examples.question_text: A map has a scale of $1:25\,000$. Two villages are $8$ cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life, in kilometres?
examples.solution_text:
Image : original is $1:25\,000$.
$\begin{align*}\text{Actual distance}&=8\times25\,000\text{ cm}\\&=200\,000\text{ cm}\\&=2000\text{ m}\\&=2\text{ km}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A model tower is built to a scale of $1:500$. The real tower is $180$ m tall. How tall is the model, in centimetres?
examples.solution_text:
Image : original is $1:500$.
$\begin{align*}\text{Model height}&=180\div500\text{ m}\\&=0.36\text{ m}\\&=36\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A recipe makes $6$ muffins using $150$ g of flour, $90$ g of sugar and $60$ g of butter. How much of each ingredient is needed for $15$ muffins?
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\text{Multiplier}&=15\div6\\&=2.5\end{align*}$
Apply the same multiplier to every ingredient.
$\begin{align*}\text{Flour}&=150\times2.5=375\text{ g}\\\text{Sugar}&=90\times2.5=225\text{ g}\\\text{Butter}&=60\times2.5=150\text{ g}\end{align*}$

(a)
$\begin{align*}\text{Total parts}&=1+2+3=6\\\text{One part}&=42\div6=7\text{ kg}\\\text{Cement}&=1\times7=7\text{ kg}\\\text{Sand}&=2\times7=14\text{ kg}\\\text{Gravel}&=3\times7=21\text{ kg}\end{align*}$
Each box represents $7$ kg.

(b)
Cement represents $1$ part; the whole batch represents $6$ parts.
$\begin{align*}1\text{ part}&=9\text{ kg}\\\text{One part}&=9\div1=9\text{ kg}\\\text{Total concrete}&=6\times9=54\text{ kg}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Leah, Max and Noor invest $\$2000$, $\$3000$ and $\$5000$ respectively in a business. They share a $\$70\,000$ profit in the same ratio as their investments. How much does each person receive?
examples.solution_text:
Divide each investment by $1000$ to find the sharing ratio.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}2000:3000:5000\\&=2:3:5\end{aligned}$
$\begin{align*}\text{Total parts}&=2+3+5=10\\\text{One part}&=\$70\,000\div10=\$7000\\\text{Leah}&=2\times\$7000=\$14\,000\\\text{Max}&=3\times\$7000=\$21\,000\\\text{Noor}&=5\times\$7000=\$35\,000\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Three friends share $\$360$. Ari receives $\frac{1}{3}$ of the money. The rest is shared between Bea and Chen in the ratio $3:5$. How much does Chen receive?
Ada, Ben and Cara share $\$390$. Ada's share to Ben's share is $5:2$. Cara receives $20\%$ more than Ada. How much does each person receive?
examples.solution_text:
Ada represents $5$ parts and Ben represents $2$ parts. Cara receives $120\%$ of Ada's share.
$\begin{align*}\text{Cara's parts}&=1.2\times5=6\\\text{Ada : Ben : Cara}&=5:2:6\\\text{Total parts}&=5+2+6=13\\\text{One part}&=\$390\div13=\$30\\\text{Ada}&=5\times\$30=\$150\\\text{Ben}&=2\times\$30=\$60\\\text{Cara}&=6\times\$30=\$180\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: An engineer draws a component using a scale of $200:1$. The drawing is $150$ cm long. What is the actual length of the component, in millimetres?
examples.solution_text:
Image : original is $200:1$, so divide the drawing length by $200$.
$\begin{align*}\text{Actual length}&=150\div200\text{ cm}\\&=0.75\text{ cm}\\&=7.5\text{ mm}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A map maker chooses a scale of $1:100$ for an area measuring $6$ km by $6$ km. Explain why this scale is unsuitable for a map intended to be carried.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\text{Map side length}&=6\div100\text{ km}\\&=0.06\text{ km}\\&=60\text{ m}\end{align*}$
The map would measure $60$ m by $60$ m, so it would be too large to carry.

examples.question_text: A $36$ kg concrete mix contains cement, sand and gravel in the ratio $1:2:3$. The whole batch is used, but the required ratio is $1:2:5$. How much extra gravel must be added?
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\text{Original total parts}&=1+2+3=6\\\text{One part}&=36\div6=6\text{ kg}\\\text{Original gravel}&=3\times6=18\text{ kg}\end{align*}$
The cement and sand stay unchanged, so one part remains $6$ kg.
$\begin{align*}\text{Required gravel}&=5\times6=30\text{ kg}\\\text{Extra gravel}&=30-18=12\text{ kg}\end{align*}$

examples.derivation: 8 × 25000 = 200000 cm; 200000 ÷ 100000 = 2 km. Matches Book 2's original-length scaling method.
180 ÷ 500 = 0.36 m; 0.36 × 100 = 36 cm. Matches Book 2's image-length method.
15 ÷ 6 = 2.5. Multiplying each ingredient by 2.5 gives 375 g flour, 225 g sugar and 150 g butter. This uses the supplied proportional-scaling method.

(a) 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 parts; 42 ÷ 6 = 7 kg per part, giving 7 kg cement, 14 kg sand and 21 kg gravel. (b) Cement is one part: 9 ÷ 1 = 9 kg per part; six parts give 54 kg total. The unshaded diagram contains exactly 1, 2 and 3 equal boxes and reveals no calculated answers.
2000:3000:5000 simplifies to 2:3:5. Ten parts share $70000, so one part is $7000. Shares are $14000, $21000 and $35000, totalling $70000. The opening ratio has the required phantom equals gutter.
Ari receives 360 ÷ 3 = $120, leaving $240. The remaining ratio has eight parts, worth $30 each; Chen receives five parts, or $150. Matches Book 2's reserved-share then remainder-sharing exercise.
Cara's parts are 1.2 × 5 = 6, giving 5:2:6. Thirteen parts share $390, so one part is $30. Ada receives $150, Ben $60 and Cara $180; Cara's share is 20% greater than Ada's.
For image:original = 200:1, actual length is 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 cm = 7.5 mm. Matches Book 2's magnified-component exercise.
Each map side is 6 ÷ 100 = 0.06 km = 60 m. A 60 m by 60 m map is unsuitable for carrying. Matches Book 2's scale-appropriateness exercise.

Six original parts share 36 kg, so one part is 6 kg. Original amounts are 6, 12 and 18 kg. Keeping cement and sand fixed requires 30 kg gravel for 1:2:5; add 30 − 18 = 12 kg. The resulting 6:12:30 simplifies to 1:2:5.
